blocks.label: Lecture introduction and learning objectives
blocks.why: The lecturer introduces the final lecture of the course and outlines the learning objectives regarding cancer therapies and their mechanisms.
blocks.content: Okay, good afternoon, everyone. Welcome to your last BOD lecture. I'm sure you'll be quite relieved to have come to the end of the BOD course. And today, we're going to finish up with a lecture on cancer therapy. And what I hope you'll be able to do by the time we've come to the end of this lecture, is to be able to summarize approaches used to treat cancer and to compare and contrast the modes of action of different cancer treatments.

blocks.label: Surgical removal and radiotherapy
blocks.why: The lecturer discusses the primary physical modalities of cancer treatment, focusing on surgical resection, margin clearance, and targeted radiotherapy.
blocks.content: So cancer therapy. It's actually really easy to kill cancer cells, and I have students in my lab who do a very good job at doing this, but of course, that's killing cancer cells in isolation. And of course, whilst we know that cancer cells are very reactive to all sorts of nasty things, it's probably not wise to do a lot of the things that people might lead you to believe are a good way of keeping yourself healthy. And therein lies, of course, the problem, which is that cancer cells are the same as your own healthy cells in many ways, and therefore, anything we do to kill them, rather paradoxically, also kills the healthy cells in our body. And this leads to all the nasty side effects that we see with a lot of cancer therapy, such as standard cytotoxic chemotherapy. And actually, the easiest way to treat cancer is to start off with the approach that just removes that mass from the body. And this is particularly good if you can generate-- conduct surgery to remove a mass, leaving clean margins. That is to say that there are no tumor cells which are left behind. So nothing that has invaded or metastasized to distant sites, because then it becomes much more difficult to conduct surgery. And surgery is often used in combination with radiotherapy. And of course, radiotherapy is a key aspect of a lot of cancer therapy, particularly things like brain tumors, where we can target the irradiation to specific sites within the brain. And of course, what that does is cause massive DNA damage, DNA strand breakage, which leads to cellular apoptosis. But early detection is very much the key to having successful surgery, detecting the tumor, as I said, before it has spread, before it has metastasized to other sites, and before it has become too invasive to the point where it's very difficult to remove it. And of course, there are some sites where it's very difficult to conduct surgery. If we think about brain tumors, for example, because getting access to the tumor can be very difficult, depending on where it is within the brain, and that surgery or procedure in itself can affect other parts of the brain which are important for our survival and normal everyday functions. And a lot of the time, chemotherapy is given alongside surgery, either perhaps beforehand to debulk the tumor, to make it more accessible, or as adjuvant chemotherapy after surgery to make sure that any little cells still hanging around, we target them with the chemotherapy following surgery.

blocks.label: Cytotoxic chemotherapy mechanisms and limitations
blocks.why: The lecturer explains how conventional cytotoxic chemotherapies damage proliferating cells and details their associated toxicities and resistance via efflux pumps.
blocks.content: Of course, the next line of defense is cytotoxic chemotherapy, and that's the chemotherapy most of us think about when we think about cancer therapy. It's those cytotoxic agents which essentially cause damage to everything that moves in your body. So these are mitotic spindle poisons, these are topoisomerase inhibitors. These are drugs which cause a lot of damage to cells, not just cancer cells, but also healthy dividing cells, causing all those side effects. But they have been the mainstay of treatment for many years now. In general, they bind either covalently or non-covalently to DNA. And many of these chemotherapy drugs can be natural compounds. And as you saw with the cancer causes lecture, we know that some things which cause lots of DNA damage and lots of destruction in cells are the very things which can cause cancer as well as we can use to treat cancer. And there are many examples of this. And if you thought back to the cancer causes lecture of all those chemicals that cause DNA adduct formation, well, we also use those drugs to kill cancer cells, but in a way that we overload the damage repair system so that the cells undergo apoptosis. So there is the potential for these drugs, of course, not to lead to apoptosis, but instead to allow cells with lower levels of DNA damage to survive, which in itself can be cancer-causing. So some of those DNA adduct-inducing agents are things like cyclophosphamide. We also use a lot of DNA cross-linking agents, such as the platinum agents, and cisplatin is one of those. Antimetabolites can also be used to treat cancer. An example of that is 5-fluorouracil. And of course, what that does is it interferes with nucleotide synthesis and ongoing cellular reproduction. And then there are the topoisomerase inhibitors. And topoisomerases, of course, are involved in that process where, when DNA is unwound and strand breakage takes place to allow replication, that process isn't repaired quite as well with topoisomerase inhibitors. And examples of that are vinca alkaloids and things like a toposide and teniposide. But chemotherapy, standard chemotherapy with cytotoxic agents, has been reasonably successful for many people, and one example of this is testicular cancer. And if you look here at this graph, this is deaths per 100,000 in Britain due to testicular cancer, and this is age at death. And you can see back in the '70s, if you were diagnosed with testicular cancer, which generally occurs in this very defined age bracket here, your chance of survival was very low. But since the introduction of cisplatin, this DNA cross-linking agent, cure rates now sit more at 90%. So you can see here, this is data from 2000 to 2004. There are very few deaths, but the incidences of testicular cancer haven't dropped. So there has been success, and of course, it's also easy to conduct surgery to treat testicular cancer because we can live without testicles. So that's another way where cancer can be treated easily if it's occurring in a part of your body which perhaps isn't essential for you to survive.

blocks.label: Limitations and systemic toxicity of cytotoxic chemotherapy
blocks.why: The lecturer moves from the clinical success of cytotoxic drugs to the challenges of combination therapy and systemic side effects.
blocks.content: But as I said, they do have their problems. One of which is we don't fully understand how they work. Not that on the individual level we don't know how they work, but we know that when we use combinations of these drugs, we really don't understand fully how they're affecting the cells in the body. And that's because over the years, we've essentially, through trial and error, put together different combinations of chemotherapeutic drugs to see what effect they have. And that has led to improved survival, as we'll come to at the end of today's lecture. And some of these drugs work synergistically, some of them perhaps work antagonistically, but we really don't understand why they work well together. And systemic toxicity is a particular problem and can be limiting in cancer treatments. So sometimes a decision is made to stop chemotherapy because of the side effects it's causing. And these can be significant from gastrointestinal toxicity, for example, because every cell that's rapidly dividing in your body is going to be hit by these cytotoxic agents as well. So you can have lots of gastrointestinal problems, of course, hair loss, lethargy, tiredness because you're killing off, not regenerating red blood cells at the same rate as would normally happen, and these are quite short-lived cells. So for someone undergoing chemotherapy, walking up the stairs can feel quite as bad as walking up Mount Everest. It can be a real effort. And some of these side effects get to the point where either you have to stop the treatment or the treatment itself can lead to death of the patient. So they're not without their issues.

blocks.label: Mechanisms of drug resistance via P-glycoprotein efflux pumps
blocks.why: The lecturer shifts to explaining the specific cellular mechanism of multidrug resistance mediated by P-glycoprotein efflux pumps.
blocks.content: Another problem with lots of cytotoxic agents is resistance. Drug resistance does develop in some cases, and largely that's through upregulation of efflux pumps. So this here is a little cartoon of an efflux pump called P-glycoprotein, which is encoded by the multidrug resistance gene, MDR1. And of course, normally, drugs diffuse into the cell through the membrane into the cytoplasm, but what these P-glycoproteins do in an ATP-dependent manner is essentially act as flipases and they just push the drug back out of the cell into the extracellular space. So you're reducing the quantity of drug in the cell and reducing its effectiveness. And people have tried to make inhibitors of these P-glycoproteins to use as a form of preventing that from happening, but inhibiting these flipases in itself is quite toxic. Because if you think about it, these are also responsible for getting rid of toxins in our cells. And so when you can't do that, you can have all sorts of effects on cells in the body as well.

blocks.label: Targeting hormone receptor signaling
blocks.why: The lecturer discusses targeted endocrine therapies that inhibit growth factor dependency in hormone receptor-positive breast and prostate cancers.
blocks.content: So where are we moving to these days? I think where we've moved to now is we're now trying to think about more targeted treatments, treatments which are very specific to the cancer cells rather than other cells in our body. And to do that, we have to think about what are the unique facets of cancer cells that we can exploit? We know, of course, that cancer cells have defects in cell cycle checkpoints. You know this from looking at the hallmarks of cancer. We know for many of these cancers, they're also genetically unstable. So you might think about ways that you could target these particular properties, which are more common in cancer cells than other cell types. So how might we design these better cancer therapies? Well, of course, as I said, if they lack key checkpoints, if they proliferate more, perhaps if they have more DNA damage, we can work on these specific vulnerabilities, and we'll come to them. But there are also some tissues, cancer tissues, which are still dependent on outside-in signaling. And if we think, for example, about breast cancer, which is estrogen receptor positive, that still requires estrogen for growth. So can we block estrogen binding to the estrogen receptor and prevent those cells from dividing? Similarly, with prostate cancer, those require androgens. Can we block androgen receptor and kill the cancer cells? Because of course, those are the ones that still need androgen for growth. And there are examples of this that are now in use. So for breast cancer, there's this drug called tamoxifen, which I'm sure many of you have heard of. And tamoxifen has had a lot of success in essentially preventing ongoing proliferation of the breast cancer cells. And we think it does this by inducing a sort of cytostatic state in the cells. So it doesn't necessarily cause apoptosis, but it prevents them from dividing. And so this is why tamoxifen can become quite a long-term treatment because when you remove the tamoxifen, the cancer cells have access to estrogen and can grow back. Similarly with prostate cancer, there are some prostate cancers that are still androgen receptor sensitive, and these, of course, can also be treated with inhibitors such as enzalutamide. So that's one way we can do it, targeting specific vulnerabilities of those cells.

blocks.label: Exploiting cell cycle checkpoint defects
blocks.why: The lecturer details how tumors with defective cell cycle checkpoints can be selectively eliminated using irradiation or engineered oncolytic adenoviruses.
blocks.content: What about those cell cycle checkpoint defects? Well, of course, we know that these checkpoint defects are really important for allowing a cell to go into cell cycle arrest and for the cell to make a decision whether it undergoes apoptosis because the damage is too much to repair, or whether to halt cell cycle and repair that damage. And of course, many cancer cells have defects in these cell cycle checkpoint proteins. We know, of course, they can lack p53, they can lack retinoblastoma. We can also lose p21 expression. We can also see loss of p16, which is often an epigenetic defect, whereby there's methylation of CpG islands in the promoters of p16. So how can we exploit that particular property in cells? Well, there was an experiment that was done quite a few years ago now, and they took a colon cancer cell line, it's called HCT116, and they took the wild-type cell line, which they hadn't genetically manipulated in any way, and then they also made the cell line so that it didn't express p21. So remember that key protein downstream of those cell cycle checkpoint responses. And what they then did was irradiate those mice that had the cells on their backs. And when they irradiated the mice, of course, the irradiation was to induce massive DNA strand breakage. What they found was that the wild type cells went in sort of a G1S arrest, and they didn't cure any of the mice of their tumors. The cells just went into a cytostatic state, and when you remove the drug, they can continue to grow. But they found the ones that lacked p21 couldn't go into cell cycle arrest and repair that damage. Instead, they underwent apoptosis, and they managed to cure almost half of the mice. So this set the scene for the fact that there were certain sensitivities of these cells to cell cycle checkpoint inhibitors and irradiation.

blocks.label: exploiting checkpoint defects using oncolytic adenoviruses
blocks.why: it explains how engineered adenoviruses can selectively kill p53-deficient cancer cells and the clinical considerations of this approach
blocks.content: So how can we exploit this in other ways? And another thing that's been done to exploit cells that lack some of these proteins is to use oncolytic viruses, in particular adenovirus. And there's a couple of adenoviruses. One is called ONIX-015 and another one called H101 that have had limited success in the clinic. But what these adenoviruses do is they rely on the fact that cells express p53 and Rb. And the adenovirus encodes two different proteins here, either E1A, which blocks Rb or E1B 55K, which blocks p53. And of course, the reason for that on an evolutionary scale is that this is an oncolytic virus, and it wants the cells to be able to enter the cell cycle so that it can produce more virions. So it does that by blocking these cell cycle checkpoint proteins. Now, you can imagine in cells which don't express p53, the E1B 55K has no target in those cells. So what if you make an adenovirus which lacks E1B 55K and you put that into cancer cells? Now, only the cells that already lack p53 will respond, because the ones that do have p53 will not have any activity because there is no E1B 55K. So in this effect, what happens is only in p53 mutant cancers through E1A blocking just Rb1, oncolytic virus replication can occur. And so this is a way of targeting the cancer cells which specifically lack p53. The problem with these adenoviruses, of course, they can cause a systemic immune response. And so this sort of thing was shown to work better if you could directly inject it into the tumor so you didn't have these sort of off-target effects on other cells in the body, these strong inflammatory responses. So again, this is another way of exploiting cancer cells which have a vulnerability because they lack this key checkpoint protein.

blocks.label: Exploiting DNA repair defects with PARP inhibitors
blocks.why: The lecturer explains the synthetic lethal strategy of using PARP inhibitors to selectively kill BRCA-deficient cancer cells that lack homologous recombination.
blocks.content: What about genetic instability? We know some cancers are genetically unstable as well because they lack DNA repair proteins. And of course, there are a number of DNA damage response pathways ranging from base excision or nucleotide excision repair, mismatch repair. But strand breakage is repaired either by non-homologous end joining when it's single breaks, or homologous recombination when it's double-strand breaks. And those processes are mediated by proteins such as PARP for single-strand breaks and the BRCA genes for double-strand breaks. So let's think about breast cancers where these patients inherit a loss of BRCA genes. Can we use that loss of the BRCA genes and that loss of ability to repair double-strand breaks to essentially treat these cells? And of course, what PARP normally does is PARP recognizes those single-strand breaks by putting these poly ADP ribose chains there, which are then recognized by the repair machinery. So if you inhibit PARP and single-strand breaks don't get repaired in the cancer cells, what happens then? Well, of course, normally when those single-strand breaks reach replication forks, they become double-strand breaks, and that's then recognized by the BRCA proteins as a double-strand break and repaired. So that's not normally a problem unless your cancer cells don't express BRCA2. And in this case, you can't repair those double-strand breaks, so when the single-strand breaks, which occur due to loss of inhibition of PARP and then become double-strand breaks at replication forks, when BRCA2 can't repair those, you get massive DNA damage through these double-strand breaks accruing and the cells undergo apoptosis. So another example where we can exploit the properties of cancer cells specifically to drive their inhibition. And this was shown by really quite a nice experiment that was conducted 20 years ago now, where you can see here this is log cell kill, and this is increasing concentration of the PARP inhibitor. And you can see in BRCA null cells that you get this nice cell death. So it's occurring really quite nice at relatively low concentrations of the PARP inhibitor. Whereas normal cells which express BRCA, they pretty much don't undergo death until you've got really, really high doses of this drug, at which point we might be seeing off-target effects or other activities. So in BRCA2 mutant cells, you pretty much have this selective effect of PARP inhibitors. And of course, PARP inhibitors are now used clinically. They were developed here in Cambridge by a company called Kudos, a spin-out from the university, and are now very successful in clinical trials, particularly in combination with other drugs.

blocks.label: Kinase inhibitors and oncogene addiction
blocks.why: The lecturer describes identifying driver mutations through genomic sequencing and designing small-molecule inhibitors to target hyperactive oncogenic kinases.
blocks.content: So we can exploit cancer cell properties. We can exploit those that have defects in cell cycle checkpoints and those which are genetically unstable. We can target those cells which are still reliant on outside in signaling by blocking binding of those outside signals, such as estrogen. But we can also think about targeted agents, and this is where a lot of research activity has been in the last 10 to 20 years, is thinking about when particular oncogenes get aberrantly activated And can we then inhibit those to cure cancer? So this led to the idea that rather than define a cancer by its location and tissue of origin, so instead of thinking of breast cancers or colon cancers, maybe we could define cancers by the oncogenic event that's driving them. So if Ras is activated, maybe we call them Rasomas. Or another example here is ALK or anaplastic lymphoma kinase, maybe we call them ALKomos. And so all cancers that have that aberrant oncogenic event could be treated with inhibitors of that particular protein. And of course, this is enabled by sequencing of cancer genomes. So when we look at all the cancer genome projects which have been going on for many years now, down the road at the Sanger Institute and also in the US, we now know a lot about the genetic landscape of different tumors and where there are driving oncogenic events. So we can look at the sequences and work out what a patient might most benefit from. And of course, these days, we also know, of course, that it's not just down to mutations in DNA, but also changes in how that genome is transcribed and changes to the epigenome. And so in the future, perhaps we'll get even better at generating these targeted therapies by looking at these cancer cells at a much deeper level. So how do we know which oncogenic events when we sequence a cancer cell is driving tumor growth? Well, there's a lot of bioinformatic processing that can be done to determine whether or not we think a particular mutation in a protein could be deleterious to the cell in which it's expressed. And often that's the case if you find something that's common amongst many different cancers. That suggests it's maybe playing a role. And this gives rise to the idea of oncogene addiction. So the idea that cancer cells are essentially addicted to that oncogenic event. So no matter what other mutations they pick up during their life and being genetically unstable, they're essentially always addicted to this original oncogenic event. And therefore, if you target that, you will be able to induce apoptosis of those cells. You might think about it similarly with loss of tumor suppressor genes, but of course, this is a little bit more complicated because we have to put a gene back into the genome. And the approaches to do that, such as gene therapy, aren't quite there yet on a larger therapeutic scale. And in fact, some of the early uses of gene therapy turned out to be oncogenic because they were using retroviruses, which of course inserted their genome into the sites of oncogenes and actually rather paradoxically led to the generation of cancer.

blocks.label: Kinase inhibitors in targeted cancer therapy and mechanisms of resistance
blocks.why: The lecturer shifts from the general concept and rationale of oncogene addiction and targeted therapy to focus specifically on targeting hyperactivated kinases, explaining inhibitor design, cross-reactivity, and resistance mutations.
blocks.content: But kinases are particularly targetable, and there are many kinases that get hyperactivated in cancer. And through looking at these kinases and knowing a little bit more about their structure, we're able to design drugs which inhibit their activity. And of course, lots of oncogenes are generated as a result of chromosomal translocations, and the one you'll be most familiar with, of course, is the Philadelphia chromosome, which generates BCR-ABL in leukemia. And this was one of the first kinases to which inhibitors were generated and used clinically to treat chronic myelogenous leukemia. NPM-ALK is another example, as is EML4-ALK, so anaplastic lymphoma kinase gets activated as a result of a translocation, in this case with nucleophosmin, and what this does is provide oligomerization domains to the kinase domain of ALK. Similarly, EML4-ALK is the consequence of an inversion event, and we see that in some lung cancers. Of course, the other way these kinases can be hyperactivated is through amplification. So for example, EGFR in lung cancer, where we have so much of the EGFR protein, it can automatically dimerize and self-activate. And then sometimes we have point mutations in kinases. So some hyperactive proteins, for example, RAF, is activated by the V600E mutant, which you had in your practical. So in the case of NPM-ALK, we're going to talk a little bit about this one because anaplastic lymphoma kinase is a receptor tyrosine kinase that sits in the membrane, and this is the transmembrane domain here. And that's what encodes the tyrosine kinase domain, which sits in the intracellular space. Now, sitting outside in the extracellular space, we have these ligand binding domains. So normally, this kinase requires some sort of ligand, which enables dimerization, autophosphorylation on SH2 domains, which of course requires ATP. Now, if you have a translocation that essentially hyperactivates this kinase by virtue of the fact that it can auto dimerize, then you don't need the ligand anymore. It becomes ligand independent. But it still requires ATP for activity. So what if you could design a drug that sits in the ATP binding pocket and prevents ATP from getting in? And that, of course, is the basis of lots of BCR-ABL and ALK kinase inhibitors. This is an ALK kinase inhibitor here called brigatinib, and it pretty much sits in that cleft where ATP normally binds and prevents ATP getting in and prevents activation of the protein. So it's very much key to having these very small molecular structures which just fit into those key binding pockets. Another example here is with epidermal growth factor receptor, EGFR, and there's a drug there called Tarceva, and that also sits in this ATP binding pocket, in this ATP cleft of the protein, prevents ATP from binding and therefore prevents activation of the protein. So these have been a real game changer in that they've provided a way to very specifically target cells which express these activated proteins, which aren't normally expressed and activated in a lot of other contexts in our body. So there are very minimal side effects. However, one of the issues with kinase inhibitors is that there are about 90 kinases in the human body, and if you look at these sort of very broad structural cartoons of these kinases, you can see they look fairly similar So actually, the ATP binding cleft of these proteins, they can be very similar and drugs that are designed for one kinase can sometimes fit into the ATP binding pocket of another kinase. So often these kinase inhibitors actually inhibit more than one kinase. Sometimes they have off-target effects in two or three different kinases, which can be an advantage because that means you can use them to inhibit more kinases, but can also lead to some off-target effects that you don't want to see. So that's one problem with these drugs or it could, depending how optimistic or pessimistic you are, might be considered a good thing. But the other issue is that resistance ultimately develops. And so patients that are on the kinase inhibitors essentially have chronic diseases now, where they have to take these kinase inhibitors for long periods of time. Because what happens is, eventually, these tumor cells can become resistant. And so normally you can see here this is actually imatinib, the BCR-ABL inhibitor sitting in ABL. And you can see here there's this threonine 315 in the ATP binding site, and that means that imatinib can sit in there quite nicely. However, some patients develop BCR-ABL with a mutation where the threonine becomes converted to an isoleucine, which of course is a different shape and has different molecular strength. And you can see here this now pokes out into that ATP binding cleft, and it actually prevents imatinib or Gleevec from getting into that ATP binding site, so these cells can become resistant to the drug. And so often this happens, but we now have second, third, and fourth generation drugs which can overcome the steric hindrance of this isoleucine here. And so sometimes patients get cycled through these different inhibitors. So when they become resistant to one, they move on to another one. And it's a bit like a whack-a-mole game because there's lots of heterogeneity within the cancer population. And so some cells might be resistant, some might be sensitive, and so you can imagine scenarios where you maybe have to cycle through the drugs to kill off different heterogeneous populations within the tumor. But ultimately, these patients have a chronic disease where they can keep the tumor at bay but essentially isn't cured.

blocks.label: Resistance mechanisms, bypass pathways, and BRAF inhibition
blocks.why: The lecturer examines secondary resistance and paradoxical drug addiction using the example of BRAF V600E inhibition and metronomic dosing strategies.
blocks.content: Now, resistance can develop by a number of other mechanisms as well, and I'm going to use the example here of RAF inhibitors. So of course, you have to remember that all of these proteins act in pathways, and so if you act in a pathway, there are multiple nodes in that pathway where you may hyperactivate the pathway if you're a cancer cell. So for example, the MAP kinase pathway can be activated very much upstream by EGF receptor amplification, for example. We know it can be activated by mutations in RAS, it can be activated by mutations in MEK, and then also we can see alternative signaling pathways which can have the same downstream effect but we use a different pathway. So activating mutations in PI3 kinase or AKT or loss of PTEN all have the same net effect of activating these pathways. So if you were to develop a drug that targets one of these pathways, you can imagine scenarios where the cells just are able to bypass that particular protein. And so activation of bypass pathways is a big problem in using targeted drugs for cancer therapy. So I'm going to talk in a little bit more detail about BRAF V600E, which of course, as you know from your practical, is mutated. So the valine is mutated to a glutamate on one allele of the protein of the gene. And of course, what that happens, what that serves to cause is that this V600E form of BRAF can function as a homodimer. It no longer needs to form heterodimers with CRAF. And of course, when heterodimers with CRAF and BRAF develop in the presence of GTP, which activates RAS, they get tethered to the membrane by farnesyltransferases. And this tethering to the membrane with GTP and this heterodimer formation serves to activate the MAP kinase pathway. So with V600E form of RAF, it's completely independent of RAS, and it can dimerize and activate the MAP kinase-- Sorry, it forms monomers and activates the MAP kinase pathway independently. And there is a drug which is designed to specifically inhibit monomers of BRAF V600E, and that's a drug called vemurafenib. And vemurafenib was used to treat melanoma very successfully. But then some strange things were being noted in the clinic. Not just resistance, and that resistance happened by a number of mechanisms. One was through amplification of that mutant form of BRAF. So essentially, we just out-compete the drug. We have so much more BRAF protein that there's not enough drug that can get into the cells to inhibit all of those copies. Another way we saw this happening was through bypass, whereby the cell started to make CRAF dimers instead of using BRAF. So it could essentially bypass BRAF completely and still activate the MAP kinase pathway. So we have amplification, we have bypass. Some cells were also seeming to mutate BRAF so they could no longer bind vemurafenib. So the cells are getting quite clever in bypassing these, and it's quite similar to how bacteria become resistant to antibiotics. They just use different pathways or mutate proteins so that they no longer are affected by the drug. Another thing that happens to bypass this is you just get hyperactivation of RAS, and hyperactivation of RAS in itself seems to actively drive MAP kinase pathway activity, but only in the presence of the drug. So this was a really strange finding because what they started to notice with some patients, that instead of inhibiting melanoma growth, they were getting rapid hyperprogressions of the tumor in the presence of drug. What could have been happening there? Well, that's exactly what was happening there, was that this V600V form of RAF could form dimers with CRAF in the presence of hyperactive RAS and drive hyperactivation of the MAP kinase pathway, and this has been termed drug addiction So essentially, the tumor cells, or at least some of the tumor cells, were becoming addicted to the drug. And again, remember, tumors are very heterogeneous, and so there are some cells which may be doing this, some cells which may have bypass pathways, some cells which might just have the V600E and still be sensitive to BRAF. So this also gave rise to the idea of using drug holidays or metronomic dosing of drugs. Because then you could go through this process where you treat the patient with the drug, the cells that are sensitive die off. You then give the cells a holiday, those that are addicted then die. Then you put the drug back on, and those that are still sensitive will die. And you can imagine a scenario where you're essentially dealing with this heterogeneous change in the tumor cell population. So metronomic or drug holidays is a way that people have been trying to use these drugs as a way to sort of prevent not only resistance but also drug addiction. And at the moment, drug addiction seems to be quite unique to kinases, but I'm sure there will be more drug addictions with other different forms of drugs being divulged in the future. So the best thing there, of course, as I said to do, is to remove vemurafenib when they become addicted. And actually, this has a better result than keep going with vemurafenib, which causes that hyperprogression. So kinase inhibitors have been very useful. They've created what has essentially become, for many patients, a chronic disease. Which is nice if you're a drug company because then you've got someone buying your drug for the rest of their life, if I want to think about it quite cynically. But it's not good if you're still suffering some side effects from these drugs. And actually, some of these kinase inhibitors, while we think they don't have many side effects, they still do. So, for example, some patients treated with ALK inhibitors are very sensitive to the sun. They have to stay out of the sunlight for the rest of their lives. So there are still side effects and this constant worry of mutations developing or resistance developing in some way.

blocks.label: Monoclonal antibodies and antibody-drug conjugates
blocks.why: The lecturer reviews therapeutic monoclonal antibodies targeting cell surface receptors and antibody-drug conjugates delivering cytotoxic payloads.
blocks.content: What are the other options? Well, the immune system. We can exploit the immune system to treat cancer. And these are mouse monoclonal antibodies. Of course, we can't give mouse monoclonal antibodies to people because they would have an immune response to that mouse monoclonal antibody. So instead, we just take the complementarity determining regions, the CDR regions that recognize a human protein, and then we put those onto a chimeric mouse human antibody. So we use the human chains. And these are antibodies that we can use to treat cancer in a number of ways. So one way is to inhibit, again, receptor activity. So, for example, there's an antibody called cetuximab, and what cetuximab does is it competes with epidermal growth factor for the epidermal growth factor receptor. And in doing so, it blocks any downstream activity of EGFR. Similarly, when we have HER2, HER2 of course, doesn't need a ligand to be activated. But what we think happens with HER2, it's bound by this monoclonal antibody called Herceptin, which we think initiates an ADCC pathway. And I'll explain that a bit more next in the context of rituximab. So rituximab is an anti-CD20 antibody. Now, CD20 is expressed on B cells, but is also expressed on a lot of B cell lymphomas, so B cell cancers. And so these B cells expressing CD20 initiate a number of responses, one being ADCC, the other being complement-mediated cytotoxicity, and the other one being ADCP or phagocytosis through macrophages. There's also this direct activity through NK cells, which can also bind to CD20 and induce cytotoxic effects on those B cells. But rituximab is quite unique. I don't think anybody really knew exactly what rituximab would do when it was first used, and we probably aren't at the heart of all the mechanisms of action of rituximab, but it works really well. The problem, of course, is that not all cancer cells express something on the cell surface, which is unique to them and them only. In fact, even CD20, of course, is also expressed on normal B cells. So patients undergoing rituximab therapy have a certain level of immunosuppression. It seems they bounce back from that when they stop treatment, but they do have immunosuppression whilst they're on the drug.

blocks.label: antibody-drug conjugates for targeted cancer therapy
blocks.why: This section introduces and details the strategy of conjugating cytotoxic drugs to monoclonal antibodies, illustrated by brentuximab delivering MMAE.
blocks.content: So another approach people have used is to target antibodies to certain proteins on the surface of cancer cells, but to link those antibodies to drugs. And so this is a targeted antibody, a targeted monoclonal antibody. An example I'm going to use today is brentuximab. Brentuximab recognizes CD30. Now, CD30 is expressed on certain cancers of the immune system, such as Hodgkin lymphoma, but CD30 is also expressed on activated B and T cells. So we do see some off-target activity. But in this case, what happens is the antibody recognizes CD30. It then gets endocytosed into the cell, where these endosomes then merge with lysosomes. And what happens then is the toxin that's bound to that antibody is released and causes activity. And in the case of brentuximab, the toxin they use is called monomethylauristatin E or MMAE, and it's a microtubule-disrupting agent. So this is a way of targeting cytotoxic chemotherapeutic drugs to cancer cells specifically. Of course, it's also going to affect activated B and T cells, but we don't see too many off-target effects with brentuximab. In fact, rather weirdly, patients treated with brentuximab get peripheral neuropathy, and we're not sure what the mechanism of that is, but it can be limiting in that we have to stop treatment because it can become too uncomfortable for the patient.

blocks.label: Evidence for immune surveillance against cancer
blocks.why: The lecturer explores historical theories and clinical evidence regarding the extent to which the adaptive immune system naturally surveils and controls tumors.
blocks.content: So we can use targeted agents, we can use antibodies, we can use kinase inhibitors, but what about exploiting our inherent immune system? Because there is an idea that our immune systems are trying to deal with cancer cells, of course, not very successfully, otherwise 50% of us wouldn't develop cancer. So where did the idea come from that our immune systems might be actively working towards eliminating cancer? Well, the early studies actually came from studies where tumor cells were being moved from one mouse to another, and these were histoincompatible mice. And actually, what they were seeing here was graft rejection rather than the immune system killing the cells. So this was sort of a misnomer in that we weren't actually seeing what we thought we were seeing, which is the immune system killing cancer cells due to them being cancer cells. Rather, it was due to them being incompatible in the host mouse. There was also this book published by Macfarlane Burnet, who came up with the immune surveillance theory of T cells, and he proposed, before we knew a lot about T cells, that T cells were there essentially to work against cancer cells. And occasionally, we do see strong tumor specific antigens, particularly in mouse models, and particularly in carcinogen-induced mouse tumors engrafted now into histocompatible mice. Although we think that often this is due to viral proteins in those tumor cells, or the expression of mutant forms of MHC. So if the immune system is doing something to protect us against cancer, surely people who are immunosuppressed should have much higher rates of cancer. And if you look at transplant patients that are on long life immunosuppressive drugs, you do see an increase, in particular in post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorders, which are considered to be driven by viruses. So it's more the fact that the body isn't able to react to those viruses rather than the tumor cells. But we also think that the kidney cancers we see in these patients might actually be due to the carcinogenic effects of immunosuppressive drugs rather than the fact that the patients don't have an active immune system. And actually, we even see some cancers decreasing in incidence in transplant patients on immunosuppressive medication. But ultimately, there's no dramatic increase in cancer overall. So this sort of argues against cancer playing a role, although the increase in cancers that we do see are largely those that are driven by viruses, so things like Kaposi's sarcoma, so of course, that's driven by HHV8, and Burkitt's lymphoma by EBV, as well as other B-cell lymphomas. So often the type of cancers we see are virally driven cancers in immunosuppressed people. So there's no evidence for a significant role for acquired immunity in the protection against non-viral cancers. But there was a study published a couple of years ago where they looked at patients that had undergone a thymectomy in adulthood. Now, the thymus is often removed during the process of cardiac surgery because it sits like a glove on the heart and it can get in the way, so often it's removed. So they followed patients that had undergone a thymectomy as adults, and they looked at cancer incidence in the population of these patients. And you can see here from this graph, this is looking at the percentage of people without cancer and years since surgery, and if you look at this blown up bit of the top end of that graph, you can see in those that had thymectomy, there were fewer patients without cancer, so more patients with cancer. It's only a small increase, but it's certainly significant and it's there. But they found that these people have more oligoclonal and less diverse TCR repertoires. So perhaps that's part of the reason as well why these thymectomized patients have a higher risk of cancer. So there's sort of anecdotal evidence for the immune system playing a role. There's also some evidence from studies like this and from patients who have undergone transplants or on immunosuppressive therapy.

blocks.label: Immune checkpoint inhibitors and neoantigens
blocks.why: The lecturer describes how checkpoint blockade antibodies reawaken exhausted T cells against tumor neoantigens and discusses immune-related toxicities.
blocks.content: But of course, the proof is in the pudding, and can you actually do something to maybe help the immune system recognize tumors and cause cancer cell death? And of course, you touched upon this in your immunology lectures, the idea of reawakening exhausted T cells. And of course, there are two signaling axes by which this can be achieved, because cytotoxic T cells are downregulated by CTLA4 and the PD-1, PD-L1 axis. So if you block these pathways with monoclonal antibodies, can you essentially reactivate the T cells to have an effect? Well, of course, CTLA4 antibodies work quite well by blocking this binding of CTLA4 to B7, and they essentially have a double effect because not only do they affect T cells, but also dendritic cells. So when you treat with PD-1 inhibitors or PD-L1 inhibitors, you can activate dendritic cells as well as activate T cells to have an effect on inducing death of your tumor cells. So the idea there is an interesting one. It relies on the fact that maybe these cells have to recognize your tumor cells in some way or form. And the early studies, well, this is one of the first studies where ipilimumab, which is an anti-CTLA4 antibody, was used clinically, and this was to treat melanoma. And you can see these are late stage patients, so of course, all new drugs have to be started in terminal patients, essentially, that have no other option in a phase one trial. So you don't expect the outcomes to be good. But they did see a striking effect in that there was this 11% increase in survival when the patients were treated with anti-CTLA4. So this was really nice. It suggested that the immune system could be doing something if we gave it the right circumstances, and we could reactivate these T cells. Unfortunately, anti-CTLA4 is highly toxic as well, because not only does it activate the T cells, which might be reacting to your tumor cells, it activates lots of other T cells in your bodies, which then attack other parts of you. And in particular, in these patients, you see something called cytokine release syndrome. And it was shown that this cytokine release syndrome is mediated by IL6. So now it's quite common to administer anti-IL6 alongside drugs such as ipilimumab. So immune checkpoint inhibitors have shown some success, and some patients do respond quite well and show quite dramatic regressions and are healthy for at least a protracted period of time. But there is toxicity. We see inflammation, we see autoimmunity, and in many of those patients, treatment with anti-CTLA4 was stopped due to these side effects. And unfortunately, 1% died due to the activities of the drug rather than the cancer. And ultimately, it may come down to the fact that you need to have a discussion with patients if you're going to be oncologists in the future about the weighing up the balance between quality of life and a few extra months of survival. But there are these responses.

blocks.label: tumor neoantigens and mutational burden in immunotherapy response
blocks.why: The lecturer shifts from checkpoint inhibitor mechanics and clinical toxicity to examine what T cells recognize, explaining tumor neoantigens and how mutation load affects treatment outcomes.
blocks.content: Now, what is it that these T cells are responding to? Are they responding to tumor antigens, and if so, what are those tumor antigens? And you might consider that the antigens that the cells are responding to are neoantigens or cells, new antigens that are generated by the tumor cells that the immune system hasn't experienced in development. And of course, lots of cancers have genetic instability, and they produce lots of mutant proteins. In particular, when we think about colon cancers associated with mismatch repair defects. And there was a nice study here which showed that to be the case. So they treated lung cancer in smokers where you see lots of mutations, and they found patients treated with ipilimumab, anti-CTLA4, did better if they had more mutations. So this is progression-free survival. So you can see more patients survive without progression if they have lots of mutations compared to the patients which had very few neoantigens. So this suggested, of course, that then the patients are responding to this treatment because they have T cells that recognize new antigens produced by the tumor cells in the form of these mutant proteins.

blocks.label: Bispecific T-cell engagers and CAR T-cell therapy
blocks.why: The lecturer explains the mechanisms, manufacturing processes, and current challenges of bispecific T-cell engagers and chimeric antigen receptor T cells.
blocks.content: What other immunotherapy approaches are there? Well, there are CAR T cells, and there are bispecific T cell engagers, and these are pretty much introduced into the clinic now, some of them showing really quite nice results, but also having some caveats of course. So bispecific T cell engagers or BiTEs are things like glofitinib. And basically, what glofitinib is, it's a single-chain variable fragment that recognizes CD3 on the T cells, and it also recognizes an antigen on the tumor cells. And this example of glofitinib, it recognizes CD20. So of course, the idea here is that you bring these cells into close proximity, hoping that these T cells will then elicit their cytotoxic activity against the tumor cell. And many of these BiTEs are in clinical trial, as I said, and are showing quite promising results. And glofitinib in particular has shown really nice results for treating adult B-cell lymphoma. But for reasons as we don't know why yet, it's not working quite so well in pediatric patients.

blocks.label: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy
blocks.why: The lecturer moves from bispecific T cell engagers to explaining the manufacturing, mechanism, challenges, and developments of CAR T cell therapy.
blocks.content: What about if you manipulate the T cells, so you make lots of T cells that recognize a tumor-specific antigen instead of hoping that they're inherently present in the body? And this is where chimeric antigen receptor T cells come into play, also known as CAR T cells, and I'm sure you've heard a lot about these in the media in recent years. But it's quite a difficult process. It's quite prolonged process as well because you have to be able to collect T cells from the patient, which requires your patient to be relatively healthy and not to be immunosuppressed due to chemotherapy. So you need a relatively healthy cancer patient who has lots of nice T cells. Then you have to isolate those T cells and transduce them to express a chimeric antigen receptor, one that recognizes a tumor-specific antigen. Then you have to expand those cells, so you've got loads of them, and then infuse them back into the patient. And this can take a long time to do. There are many examples of this, such as Kymriah, which targets CD19. It's expensive because of this whole procedure that has to happen, and it can take a month to manufacture these T cells. And there can also be multiple side effects. So you can get that cytokine release syndrome again, which is mediated by IL6. So often they have to be given with anti-IL6 as well. And rarely, there have been reports of secondary T-cell lymphomas. Maybe, though, this is due to where the chimeric antigen receptor integrates into the host genome through a retroviral transduction method, integrating to activate oncogenes. And people are working on second, third, fourth, fifth generation of CAR T cells to improve this situation. Now, it's a very crowded space at the drug company level, whereby people are looking to generate CAR T cells, which we can use off the shelf, so you don't have to worry about histocompatibility. You don't need a patient's own cells. They're now also trying to develop CAR T cells which don't get exhausted because CAR T cells, like other cells, can get exhausted. So we're looking at ways to do that, too. The other problem with these chimeric antigen receptor T cells is they don't intercalate very well into the tumor space, particularly in solid tumors. So they can work very well for liquid tumors, for example, but getting them to infiltrate into a tumor can be quite difficult, too. So there's a lot of work going on to try and improve CAR T cells, and you may also come across all sorts of other CAR type cells or even CAR Ms, CAR macrophages now. So this is a really rapidly moving space, and a lot of money is being put into immunotherapy to improve the situation that we're currently in. And actually, we're only just scratching the surface of where we could go with immunotherapy and, in fact, exploiting other aspects of the tumor microenvironment. And I showed you this picture in the last lecture, looking at all these different aspects of cell systems that are needed to support cell growth, tumor cell growth, ranging from angiogenesis, all the way through to actually immune cells and stromal cells, which may be supportive of tumor growth. So there's a lot of movement now on trying to exploit other properties and hallmarks of cancer.

blocks.label: Current challenges, biomarkers, and genomic sequencing
blocks.why: The lecturer reviews broader obstacles in cancer management, including tumor heterogeneity, trial costs, and clinical implementation of genome sequencing.
blocks.content: So cancer therapy has many challenges. Most therapies only work in some patients, and it's difficult to know which patients will respond to which drug. So we need biomarkers to help us identify the patients which will respond best to a particular drug, and those biomarkers can come in the form of monitoring cancer cells for expression of very specific proteins. And of course, we know that cancer cells can secrete DNA into the blood, into the peripheral blood, and you can look at cell-free DNA and things like this to monitor patient response. But cytotoxics can paradoxically also be cancer-causing agents, and some drugs, such as etoposide, for example, that topoisomerase inhibitor, can lead to secondary leukemias. We know that resistance develops, and when that resistance develops, we can sometimes rescue those patients with other therapies. But sometimes perhaps the patient is too sick to tolerate any further therapies by the time their disease becomes truly resistant and far more aggressive. Drug trials take a long time to run, and they're very expensive, so they cost millions and millions of pounds to run these drug trials. They have to go through multiple phases, from phase one to phase two and so on, and these take a long time to get to the clinic. But sequencing of cancer genomes is helping us to match patients to drugs. And now in the NHS, if you're a child with cancer, you have the opportunity to have whole genome sequencing conducted of your tumor so that we can ideally match that to the patient, and that's work that's being spearheaded here in our Department of Pediatric Oncology in Cambridge at Addenbrooke's Hospital, where they're also working towards an ultra-fast turnaround whole genome sequencing project so that we can get those results back to the patient before they start treatment. Of course, in the context of adults, with all the adults who have cancer, it would be very expensive to do whole genome sequencing for all of them at the moment. But we do have targeted sequencing panels looking for very specific targetable mutant proteins being expressed in those patients. However, cancer has immense plasticity, immense heterogeneity, and we know that cancer cells can evade treatment. And as I said, I mentioned all those different resistance mechanisms that we see, and those can vary in subpopulation of cells within one cancer. So we're probably moving now from a situation where we had lots of cytotoxic chemotherapists just hitting everything that moved. Then we shifted to these sort of very targeted agents that only worked on very specific proteins, but we saw lots of resistance. And now I think we're having to move back to somewhere in between all that, where we have maybe a combination of those things to prevent resistance and also not to have the significant side effects of cytotoxic chemotherapy. And whether immunotherapy will provide us with that is yet to be seen. But we've really only just begun to scratch the surface of trying to look at how we might exploit other tumor cell properties to treat cancer.

blocks.label: The role of prevention and early detection versus therapy in improving cancer outcomes
blocks.why: It examines historical improvements in cancer outcomes and attributes changes in stomach, colorectal, and lung cancer rates to prevention and screening rather than therapy alone.
blocks.content: So has therapy improved in the last 50 to 70 years? Well, it certainly has. Of course, we can't truly rule out that cancer treatment responses haven't got better due to the fact that we are better at detecting them and better at preventing them. So, for example, if we look at the rates of stomach cancer, they have decreased significantly. But of course, we worked out that many stomach cancers were being driven by Helicobacter pylori infection, and we could treat with antibiotics. Similarly, cancers of the colon and rectum, colorectal cancers, we're seeing a decrease there. And of course, we have screening programs to look at occult blood in the stools as a way of early detection. Although this is now starting to go on the uptick, where we're starting to see more cases of colorectal cancer, particularly in younger people now. And then things like lung cancer. Of course, lung cancer steadily increased with cigarette smoking. We're now seeing that also on the downturn, although we're seeing an increase in lung cancer in young women who have never smoked. So lots of environmental stimuli that may be having a role.

blocks.label: Future directions and the childhood leukemia paradigm
blocks.why: The lecturer discusses future priorities like prevention and early detection, closing with an ethical dilemma illustrated by childhood leukemia survival rates.
blocks.content: So what's next? Well, of course, we need to understand more about the biology of the cancer because this term tells us about a whole collection of hundreds of thousands of different diseases because we're all genetically different, and each cancer in a patient has gone through a very different journey in response to a different microenvironment, for example. So are we getting to the point where we're now developing more chronic diseases? And do we actually have to work more on prevention and early detection? And of course, a lot of that is ongoing, and we have, of course, the Cancer Early Detection facility here in Cambridge that is doing just that. This also raises the idea of cancer vaccines. Can we vaccinate against cancer? And there are lots of people also working on this side of things as well, although, of course, there are a whole array of cancer antigens that you might vaccinate against. So how do we do that? How do we decide what are the most important ones? Immunotherapies we've come across. Again, these might replace some of these cytotoxic drugs in the future. But we do need better biomarkers so that we can predict response. And again, there's this whole question of how a clinician should, of course, have a very good conversation with their patients at some point during their treatment stage as to whether their quality of life is perhaps not worth living when they're on some of these drugs, and maybe palliative care is a better option. Maybe we should focus more of our attention on those patients that are going to respond to therapy. So lots of ethical and moral dilemmas to think about. But I'm going to end with a success story of sorts. This is survival rates from leukemia in children, and you can see if you as a child diagnosed with leukemia back in 1970, you had a very poor rate of survival. Nowadays, over 95% of children with leukemia survive. How did we get from here to here? Well, actually, this was all hit and miss. This was trial and error in many ways, and that we started to put different combinations of cytotoxic agents together, and we found a combination that seemed to work really well. It's not due to the introduction of targeted agents, not due to the introduction of immunotherapies. And now we're in this sort of victims of our own success in many ways because we're really good at treating it with lots of cytotoxic agents. So how do you now trial targeted agents going forward? Because how do you have a conversation with the parent of a child with leukemia and say, "I have a new targeted drug, but I don't know what the survival rate's going to be like with that new targeted drug. But I do know if I treat your child with this combination of really nasty cytotoxic drugs, I'll get over 95% survival. But your child will have a life that-
